body.heading: Force spread out, or squeezed together
paragraphs: Pressure is force divided by the area it acts over. The same force can be gentle or devastating depending on how it is spread: concentrate it on a pinhead and it pierces; spread it over a wide board and it barely dents. Pressure, not force alone, decides whether things sink, cut or break.

Your body weight does not change when you put on snowshoes — but the pressure under your feet collapses. A boot presses all your weight onto a small patch of snow and punches through. A snowshoe spreads the identical weight over an area several times larger, so each bit of snow carries only a small load and holds you up.

body.heading: Sharp edges and beds of nails
paragraphs: A knife works by the opposite trick. The force from your hand is modest, but the blade's edge is microscopically thin, so the pressure at the edge is enormous — enough to force food fibres apart. A blunt knife needs a much harder push precisely because its thicker edge spreads the same force over more area.

The bed of nails is the snowshoe principle as theatre. A performer's weight spread over hundreds of nail points means each nail carries a tiny force at low pressure — uncomfortable, perhaps, but the skin is not pierced. Step on a single nail and the full force lands on one point, with the opposite result.

body.heading: Pressure in the animal kingdom and beyond
paragraphs: A stiletto heel can press on the ground harder, per square centimetre, than an elephant's foot, because the elephant's tonne-scale weight is spread over four broad pads while a person's weight on one heel tip is concentrated into a square centimetre or less. That is why heels dent soft floors and elephants do not crush the ground they walk on.

Engineers use the same arithmetic everywhere: wide tyres and tracks keep farm and military vehicles from sinking into mud, and a thumbtack's broad head protects your thumb while its point concentrates your push into the wall.
